meta.title: Who really said "If we are alone in the Universe, it sure seems like an awful waste of space"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carl Sagan's line. He quoted Thomas Carlyle at a 1972 NASA symposium; the familiar wording is dialogue from the 1997 film Contact.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If we are alone in the Universe, it sure seems like an awful waste of space'?
meta.ogDescription: Sagan credited it to Thomas Carlyle out loud in 1972. The wording everyone quotes was written for the movie Contact in 1997. Sources checked.

answer.label: Not Carl Sagan — he was quoting Thomas Carlyle
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this exact wording under Misattributed on its Carl Sagan page, calling it a paraphrase of a line Sagan himself credited to Thomas Carlyle. Opening a NASA symposium at Boston University on 20 November 1972, Sagan said that Carlyle, “upon thinking about the stars,” had said: “A sad spectacle. If they be inhabited, what a scope for misery and folly. If they be not inhabited, what a waste of space.” The phrasing people actually recognise is film dialogue — Ted Arroway’s “if it is just us… seems like an awful waste of space” in Contact (1997).

source.excerpt: Thomas Carlyle, a somewhat crusty old fellow, upon thinking about the stars, said: “A sad spectacle. If they be inhabited, what a scope for misery and folly. If they be not inhabited, what a waste of space.” I suspect that in one way or another we will be returning to those two alternatives in this discussion. Is it possible that in a universe teeming with stars and planets there is not a multitude of other inhabited worlds?
trail: 1920 — John Burroughs opens Accepting the Universe with Margaret Fuller saying she accepted the universe and Carlyle retorting “Gad, she’d better!” — then, looking up at the midnight stars: “A sad spectacle! If they be inhabited, what a scope for misery and folly; if they be na inhabited, what a waste of space!” Project Gutenberg full text ↗

20 November 1972 — Carl Sagan opens a NASA symposium at Boston University by quoting Carlyle’s two alternatives; the remarks are printed in Life Beyond Earth and the Mind of Man, NASA SP-328 (1973), p. 4. Internet Archive scan ↗

23 November 1978 — Martin Gardner opens a New York Review of Books essay with the same exclamation, in a slightly different form: “what a scope for pain and folly.” The line is loose in print well before any film. New York Review of Books ↗

1997 — Contact, directed by Robert Zemeckis from Sagan’s novel, gives the thought to Ted Arroway: “if it is just us… seems like an awful waste of space.” The screenplay is by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. Wikiquote transcript ↗
source.excerptNote: Sagan’s opening remarks as moderator. He names Carlyle, puts the sentence in quotation marks, and then builds the session around it — he is citing a line, not coining one.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular wording, because it has no traceable source work — it is a floating paraphrase, not a sentence anyone is documented as having written. The two anchor texts do have clear status: Carlyle’s exclamation as printed in John Burroughs’s Accepting the Universe (1920) is public domain in the United States, while the near-identical film dialogue in Contact (Warner Bros., 1997) and the printed 1973 symposium proceedings are modern works and should be treated as in copyright.

author.name: Thomas Carlyle
author.heading: So who was Thomas Carlyle?
author.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher whose writing shaped Victorian intellectual life — he was known in his later years as the sage of Chelsea. He is remembered for Sartor Resartus, The French Revolution: A History and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, not for astronomy. The stargazing remark that made him an accidental patron saint of SETI is not found among his published writings: it reaches us second-hand, surfacing in print in John Burroughs’s Accepting the Universe in 1920, thirty-nine years after Carlyle died in 1881.

misattribution.heading: Three layers of misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is not one bad credit but a stack of them — a paraphrase of a film line derived from a quotation of a remark that was itself only ever reported second-hand.

items.why: Wikiquote lists “If we are alone in the Universe, it sure seems like an awful waste of space” in its Misattributed section ↗, noting it is a paraphrase of Sagan quoting Thomas Carlyle. No Sagan book, essay, episode or interview is cited for the sentence anywhere on that page — and no “waste of space” line appears in its lengthy sourced section for the novel Contact (1985), which quotes the book by chapter and page throughout.

items.who: James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg, screenwriters
items.why: The recognisable phrasing is a line of movie dialogue, not a Sagan aphorism: Ted Arroway tells his daughter, “I don’t know, Sparks. But I guess I’d say if it is just us… seems like an awful waste of space.” Wikiquote transcribes the exchange ↗ and credits the screenplay to Hart and Goldenberg, working from Sagan’s novel.

Carlyle’s own line sits in Wikiquote’s Attributed section ↗ rather than among his sourced writings. The citation given is John Burroughs’s Accepting the Universe, published in 1920 — thirty-nine years after Carlyle’s death in 1881 — where it is reported as something Carlyle exclaimed while looking up at the midnight stars, not something he wrote.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence Sagan really spoke was Carlyle’s, and he said so out loud from the podium — you can read it on page 4 of the printed NASA proceedings ↗.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Sagan
lead: It is a strange piece of luck. The single sentence most people can attach to Carl Sagan’s name is one he went out of his way to attribute to somebody else. On 20 November 1972 he stood up to moderate a NASA symposium at Boston University and opened with Carlyle — “a somewhat crusty old fellow,” as Sagan put it — and the two alternatives Carlyle had posed about the stars: inhabited, and therefore a scope for misery and folly; or uninhabited, and therefore a waste of space. Sagan then built the whole session around those two alternatives.

Twenty-five years later a film made from Sagan’s own novel handed the thought back to him in tighter, warmer form. In Contact, a small girl asks her father whether there are people on other planets, and he answers that if it is just us, it seems like an awful waste of space. That line was written by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg; Sagan and Ann Druyan are credited with the story, and the film closes with a dedication reading “For Carl.” He had died in December 1996, months before release. The internet then did what it does: it smoothed the screenwriters’ dialogue into one quotable declarative, dropped the character, and stamped Sagan’s name on it.
context.detailsSummary: The wording drifts at every hand-off
detailsBody: Burroughs, 1920: “A sad spectacle! If they be inhabited, what a scope for misery and folly; if they be na inhabited, what a waste of space!” The Scots na for not survives in Burroughs’s rendering.
Sagan, 1972: “A sad spectacle. If they be inhabited, what a scope for misery and folly. If they be not inhabited, what a waste of space.” Three flat sentences; the Scots is gone.

Martin Gardner in the New York Review of Books, 1978: “If they be inhabited, what a scope for pain and folly; and if they be not inhabited, what a waste of space!” — pain, not misery, six years after Sagan and nineteen before the film.
Contact, 1997: “I don’t know, Sparks. But I guess I’d say if it is just us… seems like an awful waste of space.”
Today’s meme: “If we are alone in the Universe, it sure seems like an awful waste of space.” Nobody on that list said this.
context.pull: Sagan quoted it, a screenplay sharpened it, and the internet gave him the credit.
